source_text: Οὐ γὰρ οὕτω φοβερὸν τοῖς λύκοις τὸ ξίφος, ὡς τοῖς δαίμοσιν αἱ προσευχαὶ τῶν δικαίων. Οὐ τοίνυν μόνον ἡμεῖς πρὸς τοὺς ἁγίους μοναχοὺς ἐν ταῖς χρείαις καταφεύγομεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ βασιλεῖς αὐτοὶ πρὸς τούτους καταφεύγουσιν ἐν καιροῖς φοβεροῖς, ὥσπερ οἱ πτωχεύοντες ἐν λιμῷ πρὸς τὰς τῶν πλουσίων οἰκίας. Οὐκ Ἀχαὰβ, ὁ τῶν Ἰουδαίων βασιλεὺς, ἐν λιμῷ καὶ σιτοδείᾳ τὴν ἐλπίδα τῆς σωτηρίας εἶχεν ἐν ταῖς Ἠλίου προσευχαῖς; οὐκ Ἐζεκίας τὴν αὐτὴν ἔχων ἀρχὴν καὶ δυναστείαν, νοσῶν καὶ μέλλων τελευτᾷν, ἐφεστηκότα τὸν θάνατον ὁρῶν, ἐπὶ τὸν προφήτην κατέφυγεν, ὡς θανάτου δυνατώτερον καὶ ζωῆς χορηγόν; Καὶ μὴν καὶ πολέμου καταῤῥαγέντος, καὶ τῆς Παλαιστίνης ἐκ βάθρων αὐτῶν ἀνασπασθῆναι κινδυνευούσης, οἱ τῶν Ἰουδαίων βασιλεῖς, ἀφέντες τὴν στρατιὰν, καὶ πεζοὺς καὶ τοξότας καὶ ἱππέας καὶ στρατηγοὺς καὶ ταξιάρχους, ἐπὶ τὰς Ἑλισσαίου προσευχὰς κατέφυγον· ἡγοῦντο γὰρ αὐτοῖς ἀντὶ πολλῶν μυριάδων ἔσεσθαι τὸν θεράποντα τοῦ Θεοῦ. Τὸ δὲ αὐτὸ τοῦτο καὶ Ἐζεκίας, τοῦ Περσικοῦ πολέμου συστάντος, καὶ τῆς πόλεως περὶ τῶν ἐδάφων αὐτῶν εἰς κίνδυνον μέγιστον κατακεκλιμένης, καὶ τῶν ἐπὶ τῷ τείχει τρεμόντων καὶ δεδοικότων καὶ σειομένων, καθάπερ ἐν προσδοκίᾳ βροντῆς, ἢ σεισμοῦ πάντα κινοῦντος, τὰς Ἡσαΐου προσευχὰς ὁ βασιλεὺς ἀντέστησε ταῖς πολλαῖς τῶν Περσῶν μυριάσι· καὶ οὐκ ἐψεύσθη τῆς ἐλπίδος. Ἅμα τε γὰρ ὁ προφήτης τὰς χεῖρας ἦρεν εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν, καὶ τοῖς ἐξ οὐρανοῦ βέλεσιν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν Περσικὸν κατέλυσε πόλεμον, παιδεύων τοὺς βασιλεῖς κοινοὺς τῆς γῆς ἡγεῖσθαι σωτῆρας τοὺς ἑαυτοῦ θεράποντας, ὅπως ἂν παιδευθεῖεν, καὶ παρακαλούμενοι παρὰ τῶν δικαίων ἐπὶ πᾶσαν πρᾶξιν ἀγαθὴν καὶ φιλάνθρωπον, αἰδεῖσθαι τὰς συμβουλίας, καὶ πείθεσθαι ταῖς ἀγαθαῖς νουθεσίαις. Οὐ τοίνυν ἐκ τούτων μόνον ἔστι τὸ διάφορον ἰδεῖν ἀμφοτέρων, ἀλλὰ κἂν ἐκπεσεῖν συμβῇ καὶ τοῦτον κἀκεῖνον, τὸν μὲν τῆς ἀρετῆς, τὸν δὲ τῆς βασιλείας στερηθέντα, ὁ μὲν ῥᾳδίως ἂν ἑαυτοῦ γένοιτο, καὶ ταχέως διὰ προσευχῆς καὶ δακρύων καὶ πένθους καὶ θεραπείας πτωχῶν τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἀποτριψάμενος, πάλιν ῥᾳδίως ἐπὶ τὴν προτέραν ἀρχὴν ἀνατρέχει· βασιλεὺς δὲ ἐκπεσὼν πολλῶν μὲν ἂν δεηθείη συμμάχων, πολλῶν δὲ ὁπλιτῶν καὶ ἱππέων καὶ ἵππων καὶ χρημάτων καὶ κινδύνων· καὶ ὁ μὲν ὅλως ἐν ἑτέροις ἔχει τὴν ἐλπίδα τῆς σωτηρίας· ὁ δὲ τῇ βουλήσει καὶ τῇ σπουδῇ καὶ τῇ μεταβολῇ τῆς γνώμης ἑπομένην ἕξει τὴν σωτηρίαν εὐθέως· Ἡ βασιλεία γὰρ, φησὶ, τῶν οὐρανῶν ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστι. Καὶ μὴν ὁ θάνατος τῷ μὲν βασιλεῖ φοβερὸς, τῷ φιλοσοφοῦντι δὲ ἄλυπος· τὸν γὰρ ὑπερορῶντα πλούτου καὶ ἡδονῆς καὶ τρυφῆς, ὧν ἕνεκα ζῇν ἐπιθυμοῦσιν οἱ πολλοὶ, καὶ τὴν ἐνθένδε μετάστασιν ἀνάγκη ῥᾳδίως φέρειν. Εἰ δὲ καὶ σφαγῆναι τοῦτον συμβαίη κἀκεῖνον, ὁ μὲν ὑπὲρ εὐσεβείας ἐπισπάσεται κινδύνους, ἀθάνατον ζωὴν καὶ οὐράνιον διὰ θανάτου πραγματευόμενος· βασιλεὺς δὲ τύραννον ἕξει σφαγέα καὶ τῆς ἀρχῆς ἐραστὴν, ἐλεεινὸν θέαμα καὶ δεινὸν μετὰ τὴν σφαγὴν γινόμενος· μοναχὸν δὲ ἰδεῖν ὑπὲρ εὐσεβείας ἐσφαγμένον ἡδὺ καὶ σωτήριον θέαμα. Καὶ ὁ μὲν τοὺς ἐραστὰς τῶν οἰκείων ἀγαθῶν καὶ μιμητὰς ἕξει καὶ μαθητὰς πολλοὺς εὐχομένους αὐτῷ φανῆναι παραπλησίους· ὁ δὲ πολλοὺς ἂν ἐν προσευχαῖς ἀναλώσειεν λόγους δεόμενος τοῦ Θεοῦ μηδένα φανῆναι τῆς βασιλείας ἐραστήν.
thought_title: The monk's prayer outranks the king's sword
orientation: Chrysostom is comparing the king and the monk, showing that even kings flee to the monks' prayers in danger, and that the monk recovers more easily from falls and faces death more securely.
pass_a_gloss: For the sword is not so fearful to the wolves as the prayers of the righteous are to the demons. Not only therefore do we flee for refuge to the holy monks in our needs, but also the kings themselves flee for refuge to these in fearful times, just as those who are poor in famine flee to the houses of the rich. Did not Ahab, the king of the Jews, in famine and scarcity of grain have the hope of salvation in the prayers of Elijah? Did not Hezekiah, having the same rule and power, being sick and about to die, seeing death standing over him, flee for refuge to the prophet, as to one stronger than death and a supplier of life? And indeed also when war had broken out, and Palestine was in danger of being torn up from its very foundations, the kings of the Jews, leaving behind the army, both foot soldiers and archers and horsemen and generals and commanders, fled for refuge to the prayers of Elisha; for they considered that the servant of God would be to them instead of many tens of thousands. And this same thing also Hezekiah, when the Persian war had arisen, and the city was sinking into the greatest danger concerning its very foundations, and those on the wall were trembling and fearing and being shaken, just as in expectation of thunder, or of an earthquake moving everything, the king set the prayers of Isaiah against the many tens of thousands of the Persians; and he was not disappointed in his hope. For at the same time the prophet lifted his hands to heaven, and with the missiles from heaven God destroyed the Persian war, teaching the kings to consider his own servants common saviors of the earth, so that they might be taught, and being exhorted by the righteous to every good and humane action, to respect their counsels, and to obey their good admonitions. Not therefore from these things only is it possible to see the difference of both, but even if it should happen that both this one and that one fall, the one being deprived of virtue, the other of kingship, the one could readily become his own master, and quickly through prayer and tears and mourning and care of the poor having wiped away his sins, again readily runs back to his former rule; but a king having fallen would need many allies, and many hoplites and horsemen and horses and money and dangers; and the one has his hope of salvation wholly in others; but the other will have salvation following immediately upon his will and zeal and change of mind; For the kingdom, it says, of heaven is within you. And indeed death is fearful to the king, but to the one practicing the way of life it is without grief; for the one who despises wealth and pleasure and luxury, for the sake of which the many desire to live, must also bear the departure from here readily. And if it should happen that both this one and that one are slaughtered, the one will draw dangers upon himself on behalf of devotion to God, procuring immortal and heavenly life through death; but a king will have a tyrant as his slaughterer and a lover of his rule, becoming a pitiable and terrible spectacle after the slaughter; but to see a monk slaughtered on behalf of devotion to God is a sweet and saving spectacle. And the one will have lovers of his own good things and imitators and many disciples praying to appear similar to him; but the other would spend many words in prayers begging God that no lover of his kingship appear.

choices.term: ὁ μὲν ῥᾳδίως ἂν ἑαυτοῦ γένοιτο
choices.english: the one could readily become his own master
choices.why: ἑαυτοῦ γένοιτο means 'become his own master' or 'regain himself,' indicating recovery of autonomy and virtue, not mere self-improvement
rejected: the one could readily recover himself

choices.term: ἀθάνατον ζωὴν καὶ οὐράνιον διὰ θανάτου πραγματευόμενος
choices.english: procuring immortal and heavenly life through death
choices.why: πραγματευόμενος means 'procuring/acquiring by effort,' not 'effecting'; the monk secures life, not causes it
rejected: effecting immortal and heavenly life through death

choices.term: τὰς Ἡσαΐου προσευχὰς ὁ βασιλεὺς ἀντέστησε
choices.english: the king set the prayers of Isaiah against
choices.why: ἀντέστησε means 'set against' as a counter-force, matching the military imagery of the passage
rejected: the king opposed the prayers of Isaiah to

choices.term: παιδεύων τοὺς βασιλεῖς κοινοὺς τῆς γῆς ἡγεῖσθαι σωτῆρας τοὺς ἑαυτοῦ θεράποντας
choices.english: teaching the kings to consider his own servants common saviors of the earth
choices.why: παιδεύων means 'teaching/instructing,' and κοινοὺς σωτῆρας means 'common saviors,' preserving the universal scope
rejected: instructing the kings to regard his own servants as common saviors of the earth

choices.term: τῇ βουλήσει καὶ τῇ σπουδῇ καὶ τῇ μεταβολῇ τῆς γνώμης ἑπομένην ἕξει τὴν σωτηρίαν εὐθέως
choices.english: will have salvation following immediately upon his will and zeal and change of mind
choices.why: ἑπομένην means 'following upon,' indicating salvation follows as a consequence of the monk's will, zeal, and change of mind
rejected: will have salvation immediately following his will and zeal and change of mind

choices.term: ὁ μὲν ὑπὲρ εὐσεβείας ἐπισπάσεται κινδύνους
choices.english: the one will draw dangers upon himself on behalf of devotion to God
choices.why: ἐπισπάσεται means 'will draw upon himself,' indicating the monk actively invites dangers for the sake of devotion to God
rejected: the one will incur dangers on behalf of devotion to God

pass_b_english: For the sword is not so terrifying to wolves as the prayers of the righteous are to demons. So it is not only we who flee for refuge to the holy monks in our times of need; kings themselves flee to them in fearful seasons, just as the poor in a famine flee to the houses of the rich. Did not Ahab, the king of the Jews, in famine and scarcity of grain, place the hope of his salvation in the prayers of Elijah? Did not Hezekiah, who held the same rule and power, when he was sick and about to die and saw death standing over him, flee to the prophet as one stronger than death and a supplier of life? And indeed, when war broke out and Palestine was in danger of being torn up from its very foundations, the kings of the Jews abandoned the army—the infantry, the archers, the cavalry, the generals, and the commanders—and fled to the prayers of Elisha. For they considered the servant of God to be worth many tens of thousands. Hezekiah did the same thing when the Persian war arose and the city had sunk into the greatest danger of being razed to its foundations, and those on the wall were trembling, afraid, and shaken as if in expectation of thunder or an earthquake moving everything. The king set the prayers of Isaiah against the many tens of thousands of the Persians, and he was not disappointed in his hope. For as soon as the prophet lifted his hands to heaven, God destroyed the Persian war with weapons from heaven, teaching the kings to consider his own servants common saviors of the earth, so that they might be instructed, and when they were called upon by the righteous to every good action and work of love for humanity, they might respect their counsels and obey their good admonitions.

It is possible to see the difference between the two not only from these things, but also if it happens that both fall—the one deprived of kingship, the other of virtue. The monk can readily become his own master, and quickly, through prayer and tears and mourning and care for the poor, wipe away his sins and run back readily to his former rule. But a king who has fallen would need many allies, many hoplites, horsemen, horses, money, and would face many dangers. The king altogether has his hope of salvation in others; the monk will have salvation following immediately upon his will and zeal and change of mind. For it says, "The kingdom of heaven is within you" (Luke 17:21). And indeed, death is fearful to the king, but painless to the one who follows the way of life. For the one who despises wealth and pleasure and luxury—the things for whose sake most people desire to live—must also bear departure from this world readily. And if it happens that both are slain, the one will draw dangers upon himself on behalf of devotion to God, procuring immortal and heavenly life through death. But a king will have a tyrant as his slayer, a lover of his power, and after the slaughter he becomes a pitiful and terrible sight. To see a monk slain on behalf of devotion to God, however, is a sweet and saving sight. And the one will have many lovers and imitators and disciples of his own good things, praying that they may appear like him. But the other would spend many words in prayers, begging God that no lover of his kingship may ever appear.

problems.quote: the city was in the greatest danger of collapsing upon its own foundations
problems.source_quote: τῆς πόλεως... εἰς κίνδυνον μέγιστον κατακεκλιμένης
problems.why: κατακεκλιμένης means 'lying prostrate/collapsed,' not 'in danger of collapsing'; the city had already fallen prostrate in danger.
problems.fix: the city lying prostrate in the greatest danger upon its own foundations
problems.ruling: κατακεκλιμένης is perfect passive participle: 'having been laid prostrate,' not future danger of collapsing.

problems.quote: the one deprived of virtue, the other of kingship
problems.source_quote: τὸν μὲν τῆς ἀρετῆς, τὸν δὲ τῆς βασιλείας στερηθέντα
problems.why: The monk is deprived of kingship, the king of virtue; the English reverses the assignment by pairing 'the one' with virtue.
problems.fix: the one deprived of kingship, the other of virtue
problems.ruling: Greek τὸν μὲν τῆς ἀρετῆς...τὸν δὲ τῆς βασιλείας: monk lacks virtue, king lacks kingship; English reverses.

problems.quote: many soldiers, horsemen, horses, money, and dangers
problems.source_quote: πολλῶν μὲν ἂν δεηθείη συμμάχων, πολλῶν δὲ ὁπλιτῶν καὶ ἱππέων καὶ ἵππων καὶ χρημάτων καὶ κινδύνων
problems.why: ὁπλιτῶν means 'hoplites/heavy-armed infantry,' not generic 'soldiers'; καὶ κινδύνων means 'and would face many dangers,' not that dangers are things he needs.
problems.fix: many allies, many hoplites, horsemen, horses, money, and would face many dangers
problems.ruling: ὁπλιτῶν = 'hoplites,' specific heavy infantry; καὶ κινδύνων = 'and [face] dangers,' not resources needed.

problems.quote: The one has his hope of salvation entirely in others
problems.source_quote: ὁ μὲν ὅλως ἐν ἑτέροις ἔχει τὴν ἐλπίδα τῆς σωτηρίας
problems.why: This refers to the fallen king, not 'the one' (the monk); the English 'The one' is ambiguous and could refer to the monk just described.
problems.fix: The king has his hope of salvation entirely in others
problems.ruling: ὁ μὲν refers to king (last masculine subject in contrast pair); English 'The one' wrongly points to monk.

problems.quote: the other will have salvation following immediately upon his will and zeal and change of mind
problems.source_quote: ὁ δὲ τῇ βουλήσει καὶ τῇ σπουδῇ καὶ τῇ μεταβολῇ τῆς γνώμης ἑπομένην ἕξει τὴν σωτηρίαν εὐθέως
problems.why: This refers to the monk, but 'the other' is ambiguous after the previous sentence's 'The one'/'the other' pairing was reversed.
problems.fix: the monk will have salvation following immediately upon his will and zeal and change of mind
problems.ruling: ὁ δὲ refers to monk, but after sentence 7's reversal, 'the other' is structurally ambiguous/misleading.

problems.why: Glossary bans 'humane'; requires 'love for humanity' or related sense per glossary.
problems.ruling: φιλάνθρωπον means 'loving mankind'; 'humane' is a distinct modern concept, potentially misleading.

problems.quote: The king has his hope of salvation entirely in others

fixed.quote: the city lying prostrate in the greatest danger upon its own foundations
fixed.fix: the city had sunk into the greatest danger of being razed to its foundations
fixed.note: The English makes the city 'prostrate upon its foundations' and breaks the sentence's grammar; περὶ τῶν ἐδάφων means danger to its very foundations, and the proposed fix keeps the broken grammar.

dismissed.why: κοινοὺς here means 'shared' or 'universal,' not 'common' in the sense of ordinary; God teaches kings to view his servants as saviors for all people.
dismissed.note: 'Common saviors of the earth' already means saviors shared by all, so the change is only a matter of style.

dismissed.quote: the one will have many lovers and imitators and disciples of his own good things
dismissed.why: The syntax groups 'lovers of his own good things' together; 'disciples of his own good things' is awkward and misleading—μαθητὰς is parallel to ἐραστὰς and μιμητάς, all taking the genitive.
dismissed.note: The genitive can reasonably govern all three nouns, and the English reads acceptably.
